title: Anurag Kashyap Called Imtiaz Ali a 'Muttonkhor' on His Birthday. It Was the Most Loving Insult of the Year.
excerpt: On June 16, Imtiaz Ali turned 55 — and the industry quietly admitted the man who taught the diaspora how to fall in love is newer than ever.
body:
There's a particular kind of love letter that only one filmmaker can write to another, and on June 16 — **Imtiaz Ali**'s 55th birthday — **Anurag Kashyap** wrote the year's best one. It was savage, tender, and so specific that it could only have come from someone who has spent two decades watching this man break hearts for a living.

The post went up on Instagram first thing in the morning: a dramatic black-and-white close-up of Ali, and a caption that read like a roast and a benediction at once. Kashyap called him "fresh, brand new" — a wink at a director on his fifth act feeling like a debutant again — and then, with the timing of a man who knows exactly what he's doing, signed off by calling him **"Muttonkhor."** Loosely: glutton, mutton-eater, a Lucknowi term of endearment dressed up as an insult. The internet lost it. "That Muttonkhor was personal," one fan wrote, and they weren't wrong.

> "Go watch it and I love you, Muttonkhor. Keep inspiring and breaking our hearts. Aur mere humdumon ko chori karna band karo, humein bhi kaam karna hai." — Anurag Kashyap

That last line — *stop stealing my favourite collaborators, I've got work to do too* — is the kind of joke only real affection earns. Kashyap was needling Ali for the team behind his latest, **Main Vaapas Aaunga**: composer **A.R. Rahman**, lyricist Irshaad Kamil, cinematographer Sylvester Fonseca. "Kudos to your partners in this heartbreaking crime," he closed, and the metaphor did double duty. An Imtiaz Ali film *is* a heartbreaking crime. You walk in whole and walk out wrecked, humming the soundtrack.

https://www.instagram.com/p/DZobJzIBbNI/

But the genuinely revealing thing Kashyap did was a feat of editorial sleight-of-hand: he called *Main Vaapas Aaunga* Imtiaz Ali's **"second film."** Not his tenth. His second. The first, in Kashyap's reckoning, was 2024's *Amar Singh Chamkila* — the Diljit Dosanjh biopic that topped Netflix's global charts and resurrected Ali's reputation after the wilderness years. It's a pointed bit of mythmaking, and it tells you how the industry has quietly recalibrated around this director: there was Imtiaz Before, and there is Imtiaz Now.

The Before is the stuff of diaspora canon. **Jab We Met** taught a generation how to fall in love on a train. **Rockstar** gave Ranbir Kapoor his most tortured, electric register and handed Rahman a soundtrack people still cry to in Edison and East London. **Tamasha**, **Highway**, the original **Love Aaj Kal** — these are the films NRIs grew up rewatching on grainy DVDs and later, guiltily, on dodgy streams. Ali's gift was never plot. It was the ache of a person trying to become themselves, usually while travelling somewhere, usually to a tune that wouldn't leave your head.

Then came the slump. *Jab Harry Met Sejal* underwhelmed. The 2020 *Love Aaj Kal* reboot was so poorly received he has all but disowned it. For a while, the auteur looked stranded by his own template. Which is exactly why *Chamkila* landed like a thunderclap — and why *Main Vaapas Aaunga*, his Partition-era love story with **Diljit Dosanjh**, **Sharvari** and **Vedang Raina**, has the industry leaning in.

The birthday tributes piled up through the day. **Kartik Aaryan** — reportedly in talks for an Ali project of his own — called the filmmaker a "visionary" in a heartfelt post. Ali's *Chamkila* collaborator Tahira Kashyap said *Main Vaapas Aaunga* left her in tears and called it "a classic love story." Anjana Sukhani, who acted in his earlier films, described working with him as "the most fulfilling experience." For a director who spent a few years being eulogised in the past tense, the room has very much turned back toward him.

The film itself is finding its feet commercially — it opened to a modest ₹5.63 crore weekend, behind the 3D horror spoiler *Haunted: Echoes of the Past*, in a brutally crowded June. But the reviews have been warm, the Rahman album dropped in full on June 15, and Ali has never been a first-weekend filmmaker anyway. His movies are slow burns that live forever on streaming and in the hearts of people who keep meaning to "take a trip and find themselves."

Fifty-five, then, and somehow newer than ever. The "fresh brand new" jab cuts deeper than Kashyap probably intended. Because the thing about Imtiaz Ali is that he keeps writing the same film — about longing, about the road, about the self you're terrified to become — and somehow it keeps landing as if for the first time. Long may he keep breaking our hearts. Muttonkhor and all.
